title: How do frameworks like Spring, JPA, and JUnit use annotations at runtime (scanning for `@Component`/`@Entity`/`@Test` via reflection + classpath scanning), and how does annotation processing at compile time differ (`javax.annotation.processing.Processor`, code generation, e.g. Lombok/MapStruct)?
shortTitle: How do Spring, JPA, and JUnit use annotations at runtime?

s1_definition.profdef: An annotation is metadata attached to code that a tool reads to decide behaviour. Frameworks such as Spring, JPA (Hibernate), and JUnit read annotations at runtime by scanning the classpath and using reflection to discover classes and members marked with `@Component`, `@Entity`, or `@Test`, which requires those annotations to have `@Retention(RUNTIME)`. Compile-time annotation processing is a completely different mechanism: an annotation processor implementing `javax.annotation.processing.Processor` runs inside `javac` during compilation, reads `SOURCE`-retained annotations, and generates new source files or validates code before any bytecode exists; Lombok and MapStruct work this way.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of annotations as coloured stickers on bank forms. Runtime scanning is like a manager walking through the office each morning, looking at every desk, and finding the forms with a red "process this" sticker so work can begin while the bank is open. Compile-time processing is like the printing press that, before the forms ever reach a desk, reads a "generate a carbon copy" sticker and prints extra paperwork automatically. One happens live while the bank runs, the other happens in the factory before anything ships.
s1_definition.oneliner: Runtime annotations are read by reflection while the program runs, compile-time annotations are read by `javac` plugins that generate or check code before the program exists.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** An annotation is metadata attached to code that a tool reads to decide behaviour. Frameworks such as Spring, JPA (Hibernate), and JUnit read annotations at runtime by scanning the classpath and using reflection to discover classes and members marked with `@Component`, `@Entity`, or `@Test`, which requires those annotations to have `@Retention(RUNTIME)`. Compile-time annotation processing is a completely different mechanism: an annotation processor implementing `javax.annotation.processing.Processor` runs inside `javac` during compilation, reads `SOURCE`-retained annotations, and generates new source files or validates code before any bytecode exists; Lombok and MapStruct work this way.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of annotations as coloured stickers on bank forms. Runtime scanning is like a manager walking through the office each morning, looking at every desk, and finding the forms with a red "process this" sticker so work can begin while the bank is open. Compile-time processing is like the printing press that, before the forms ever reach a desk, reads a "generate a carbon copy" sticker and prints extra paperwork automatically. One happens live while the bank runs, the other happens in the factory before anything ships.

**One line to remember:** Runtime annotations are read by reflection while the program runs, compile-time annotations are read by `javac` plugins that generate or check code before the program exists.

sections.s2_technical:
When Spring boots, component scanning walks the configured base packages, loads class metadata, and asks each class whether it carries a stereotype annotation. It does this with reflection. For example, `clazz.isAnnotationPresent(Service.class)` returns true for a class marked `@Service`, and Spring then registers a bean definition for it. A small illustration: if you have `@Service class TransferService {}`, Spring effectively runs `TransferService.class.getAnnotation(Service.class)` and, because the result is not null, creates and manages a single instance.

JPA and Hibernate do the same at startup to build the persistence metamodel. Hibernate reads `@Entity`, `@Table`, `@Id`, and `@Column` through reflection to learn how a Java class maps to a database table. For instance, `Trade.class.getAnnotation(Table.class).name()` would yield `"trades"` so Hibernate knows which table to insert into. All of this only works because these annotations declare `@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)`, which tells the compiler to keep them inside the `.class` file where reflection can see them.

JUnit 5 discovers tests the same way. Its engine scans test classes and, for each method, checks `method.isAnnotationPresent(Test.class)`; when true it invokes that method as a test. You can see the dependency on retention clearly: if `@Test` were `SOURCE`-retained it would be erased after compilation and JUnit would find nothing to run.

Compile-time annotation processing is a separate world that happens inside the compiler. You write a class that extends `AbstractProcessor` (which implements `javax.annotation.processing.Processor`), declare which annotations it handles with `@SupportedAnnotationTypes`, and register it so `javac` loads it. During compilation `javac` calls your processor's `process` method, handing you the set of program elements carrying your annotation through the `RoundEnvironment`. A tiny example of reading them: `roundEnv.getElementsAnnotatedWith(GenerateAudit.class)` returns the methods marked `@GenerateAudit`, and you can then emit a brand new Java file with `processingEnv.getFiler().createSourceFile("AuditProxy")`.

MapStruct uses this to turn a mapper interface into a fully written implementation class at compile time, so there is zero reflection at runtime and the mapping is as fast as hand-written code. Lombok uses a more aggressive variant that mutates the compiler's abstract syntax tree directly, so writing `@Getter` on a field makes the getter appear in the compiled class even though you never typed it. The key senior-level nuance is the trade-off: runtime reflection is flexible and dynamic but costs startup time and offers no compile-time safety, whereas compile-time processing costs nothing at runtime, fails fast with real compiler errors, but cannot react to configuration discovered only when the program runs.
sections.s3_banking:
At National Bank of India we have two customers whose records we keep working with: Rajesh, a software engineer with savings account SAV2001 holding ten lakh rupees, and Priya, a property owner with current account CUR3001 holding two lakh fifty thousand rupees.

Problem 1 — the bank keeps adding new kinds of services (transfer, fraud check, interest), and a human wiring each one together by hand is error-prone and slow. We want to mark a class once and have the system find it and create it for us. This is exactly how runtime annotation scanning works: we invent a marker annotation, keep it with `RUNTIME` retention, and at startup we scan a list of candidate classes, use reflection to spot the marker, and instantiate those classes automatically into a tiny container.

Problem 2 — auditors demand that every money-moving method be logged, and developers keep forgetting to write the log line. Instead of trusting people, we want the build itself to notice a method marked "must be audited" and react before the program even runs. This is exactly how compile-time annotation processing works: we write a processor that `javac` runs, and it reports a compiler-level note for every method carrying our audit marker, proving the marker was read during compilation and not at runtime.

Our runnable demo will define a `RuntimeComponent` annotation retained at `RUNTIME`, a `CompileAudit` annotation retained at `SOURCE`, an `Account` domain class with debit and credit, a `TransferService` marked as a runtime component, a very small `MiniContainer` that scans a class list and builds beans by reflection, and a `main` method that proves Spring-style discovery works by finding and running the transfer. We will also show the separate annotation-processor class and the bash command that registers it, so the compile-time path is complete.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Register the processor so javac loads it
# File content of META-INF/services/javax.annotation.processing.Processor:
#   com.bank.annotations.processor.AuditAnnotationProcessor

# Compile the processor first (it must exist before it can process other code)
javac -d out src/main/java/com/bank/annotations/processor/AuditAnnotationProcessor.java

# Compile the app WITH the processor on the classpath; watch for the NOTE lines
javac -cp out -processorpath out -d out src/main/java/com/bank/annotations/*.java

# Run the runtime-scanning demo
java -cp out com.bank.annotations.AnnotationScanDemo
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a list of candidate classes `[TransferService.class, Account.class]`, plus Rajesh (SAV2001, balance 1000000) and Priya (CUR3001, balance 250000), and a rent amount of 50000.

Step 1 — the container receives the candidate list. At this moment nothing is instantiated; the classes are just metadata loaded by the JVM. The container will decide which deserve to become beans.

Step 2 — for each candidate the container calls `isAnnotationPresent(RuntimeComponent.class)`. This reflective check reads the `.class` file metadata. Because `RuntimeComponent` is `RUNTIME`-retained, the marker survived compilation and the check returns true for `TransferService` and false for `Account`.

Step 3 — `TransferService` passes the check, so the container calls its no-argument constructor by reflection and stores the single instance in its bean map. The bean count becomes one. `Account` is skipped and logged at the fine level.

Step 4 — the demo asks the container for the `TransferService` bean. It returns the exact instance created in step 3, so the application uses a managed object it never explicitly constructed, which is the essence of inversion of control.

Step 5 — `transfer` runs. Rajesh is debited 50000, moving his balance from 1000000 to 950000, and Priya is credited 50000, moving hers from 250000 to 300000. The success is logged. Separately, back at compile time, the annotation processor had already printed a note for this same `transfer` method because of its `@CompileAudit` marker.

Final output:

```text
2026-10-30 19:20:01 INFO    Registered bean: TransferService
2026-10-30 19:20:01 INFO    Beans discovered by reflection scan: 1
2026-10-30 19:20:01 INFO    Transfer 50000 from SAV2001 to CUR3001 SUCCESS
2026-10-30 19:20:01 INFO    Rajesh balance now: 950000
2026-10-30 19:20:01 INFO    Priya balance now: 300000
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Annotations are metadata attached to code, and the crucial thing I always clarify in an interview is that two completely different machines read them at two completely different times. Frameworks like Spring, Hibernate, and JUnit read annotations at runtime. When the application starts, Spring scans the configured packages, loads class metadata, and uses reflection to find every class marked with a stereotype like at-Service or at-Component, then creates and manages those objects for you. Hibernate does the same with at-Entity and at-Table to learn how a class maps to a database table, and JUnit checks each method for at-Test before invoking it. All of this only works because those annotations are retained at runtime, which tells the compiler to keep the marker inside the compiled class file where reflection can still see it.

Compile-time annotation processing is a different mechanism entirely. Here you write a class that extends AbstractProcessor, which implements the processing Processor interface, and the Java compiler itself loads and runs it during compilation. The processor is handed every program element carrying the annotations it cares about, and it can either validate the code and raise real compiler errors or generate brand new source files. MapStruct uses this to write a complete mapper implementation at build time, so there is no reflection cost at runtime, and Lombok uses a similar hook to add getters and setters into the compiled class even though you never typed them.

The trade-off is what shows seniority. Runtime reflection is flexible and can respond to configuration discovered only when the program is running, but it costs startup time and gives no compile-time safety. Compile-time processing costs nothing at runtime and fails fast with proper compiler errors, but it cannot react to anything that is only known live.

In our banking platform at National Bank of India I used both. I built a small component marker retained at runtime so a lightweight container could scan candidate classes and automatically discover and instantiate the transfer service, exactly the way Spring discovers a service, which meant developers never wired money-moving services by hand. Separately, to satisfy auditors, I wrote a compile-time annotation processor that scans for an audit marker on every method that moves money and reports it during the build, so a developer who forgets the audit requirement finds out at compile time rather than in production. Seeing the same transfer method get discovered by reflection at runtime and flagged by the processor at compile time is the clearest way I know to explain that annotations themselves are just stickers; it is the reader, and when it reads, that defines everything.

---

keyPoints: JPA: @Entity/@Column — Hibernate reads annotations to map objects to tables
JUnit: @Test — test runner discovers methods via reflection
All depend on @Retention(RUNTIME) — annotations must survive compilation
Compile-time processing: Lombok uses SOURCE retention + annotation processor
